title: Ibn Taymiyyah
hookLine: a Damascus scholar of the Mongol age, influential and debated, who called for return to early sources

cards: A question arrives at a scholar's door in Damascus. It concerns a town called Mardin. Its people are Muslims, but the power over them now belongs to the Mongols, whose armies have been raiding toward Syria.

So which is it: a land of peace, or a land of war? The answer decides how people there are to be treated, and what they owe. The scholar gives an answer that fits neither box, and readers have argued over it ever since.

teach.h: A SCHOLAR OF THE MONGOL AGE.
teach.b: Ibn Taymiyyah taught in Damascus in the age of the Mongol raids, a scholar of the Hanbali school, sharp, prolific, and not one to avoid a fight.
His great call was to go back to the sources: the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the way of the earliest generations of Muslims, the salaf. Back past the layers, to the beginning.
His answer on Mardin shows the kind of distinction he drew.

teach.h: MARDIN: NOT PEACE, NOT WAR, A THIRD KIND.
teach.b: The town, he said, was neither simply a land of peace nor simply a land of war, but a third kind, a mixture. The Muslims there were to be treated as Muslims, and those who had left the path as their conduct deserved.
The question offered two colors, and he refused to paint with only two. His life was not quiet.
He clashed with rulers and with other scholars, and was imprisoned more than once; his student Ibn Kathir records that he died a prisoner in the citadel of Damascus. His name is still argued over.
Some Muslims call him Shaykh al-Islam and read him closely. Others, including theologians and Sufis, have disagreed with him sharply on important points.
And in modern times his words have been quoted for very different purposes, sometimes cut loose from their questions.

Hence today's line: read him in his age. A ruling written for a town under Mongol power, by a man watching armies on the border, has to be read with that town and those armies in view. That's true of any scholar.
Know the question before you judge the answer.

how: Students of Islamic law and theology read Ibn Taymiyyah's fatwas and treatises alongside those of scholars who disagreed with him, and teachers stress reading each ruling with the question and setting that produced it.

games.q: you're Ibn Taymiyyah. people ask whether Mardin, a Muslim town under Mongol power, is a land of peace or a land of war. what do you answer?
o: neither: a third kind, a mixture.
games.why: he refused the two boxes. Muslims there were to be treated as Muslims, and others as their conduct deserved.

practice: Think of a writer or public figure you feel strongly about, for or against, mostly from what others say, and be honest about how much of their own words you've read.

Take one thing they said and ask: who were they answering, when, and what was happening around them? If you pray, ask Allah for fairness in how you judge; if not, simply notice how much the answers might change.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Taymiyyah. A Damascus scholar of the Mongol age who called people back to the early sources, admired by some, debated by others. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: son of Taymiyyah, a family name; reports differ on who Taymiyyah was.
